claim: 5-Methylcytosine (m5C) is one of the posttranscriptional modifications in mRNA.
source: 5-Methylcytosine (m5C) is one of the posttranscriptional modifications in mRNA and is involved in the pathogenesis of various diseases.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about m5C.

claim: m5C is involved in the pathogenesis of various diseases.
source: 5-Methylcytosine (m5C) is one of the posttranscriptional modifications in mRNA and is involved in the pathogenesis of various diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about m5C.

claim: DRAM is an antibody-free and bisulfite-free approach for m5C detection.
source: This antibody-free and bisulfite-free approach provides transcriptome-wide editing regions which are highly overlapped with the publicly available bisulfite-sequencing (BS-seq) datasets and allows for a more stable and comprehensive identification of the m5C loci.
evidence: The manuscript describes the technical characteristics of the DRAM method.

claim: DRAM provides transcriptome-wide editing regions that are highly overlapped with publicly available BS-seq datasets.
source: This antibody-free and bisulfite-free approach provides transcriptome-wide editing regions which are highly overlapped with the publicly available bisulfite-sequencing (BS-seq) datasets and allows for a more stable and comprehensive identification of the m5C loci.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published BS-seq data.

claim: DRAM system supports ultralow input RNA (10 ng).
source: In addition, DRAM system even supports ultralow input RNA (10 ng).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in the manuscript.

claim: More than 170 RNA modifications have been identified.
source: More than 170 RNA modifications have been identified, mainly including m6A, m5C, m1A, m7G, and others (Wiener and Schwartz, 2021; Li and Mason, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RNA m5C methylation is observed across different RNA types including tRNA, mRNA, rRNA, vault RNA, microRNA, long noncoding RNA, and enhancer RNA.
source: Notably, RNA m5C methylation represents a crucial posttranscriptional modification observed across different RNA types, such as tRNA, mRNA, rRNA, vault RNA, microRNA, long noncoding RNA, and enhancer RNA (Van Haute et al., 2019; Blaze et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2013; Hussain et al., 2013; Aguilo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: m5C has multiple molecular functions in key stages of RNA metabolism including mRNA stability, translation, and nuclear export.
source: Numerous studies have revealed multiple molecular functions of m5C in numerous key stages of RNA metabolism, such as mRNA stability, translation, and nuclear export (Yang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019; García-Vílchez et al., 2019; Trixl and Lusser, 2019; Boo and Kim, 2020; Courtney et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Dynamic alterations of m5C play integral roles in early embryonic development.
source: The dynamic alterations of m5C play integral roles in many physiological and pathological processes, such as early embryonic development (Liu et al., 2022), neurodevelopmental disorder (Chen et al., 2019b; Flores et al., 2017), and multifarious tumorigenesis and migration (Chen et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2019a; Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: Dynamic alterations of m5C play integral roles in neurodevelopmental disorder.
source: The dynamic alterations of m5C play integral roles in many physiological and pathological processes, such as early embryonic development (Liu et al., 2022), neurodevelopmental disorder (Chen et al., 2019b; Flores et al., 2017), and multifarious tumorigenesis and migration (Chen et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2019a; Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2019b and Flores et al., 2017.

claim: Dynamic alterations of m5C play integral roles in tumorigenesis and migration.
source: The dynamic alterations of m5C play integral roles in many physiological and pathological processes, such as early embryonic development (Liu et al., 2022), neurodevelopmental disorder (Chen et al., 2019b; Flores et al., 2017), and multifarious tumorigenesis and migration (Chen et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2019a; Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on cancer.

claim: m5C modification significantly contributes to the regulation of gene expression.
source: Moreover, this modification significantly contributes to the regulation of gene expression (Yang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019; García-Vílchez et al., 2019; Trixl and Lusser, 2019; Boo and Kim, 2020; Courtney et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Bisulfite-sequencing (BS-seq) has been proven to be the gold standard method for RNA m5C methylation analysis.
source: To date, bisulfite-sequencing (BS-seq) has been proven to be the gold standard method for RNA m5C methylation analysis (Yang et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019; Trixl et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies establishing BS-seq as the standard.

claim: BS-seq chemically deaminates unmethylated cytosine to uracil while keeping methylated cytosine unchanged.
source: This approach chemically deaminates unmethylated cytosine to uracil, while keeping methylated cytosine unchanged.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of BS-seq.

claim: Bisulfite treatment in BS-seq is extremely detrimental to RNA, resulting in unstable detection of m5C in low abundance RNA or highly structured RNA.
source: However, bisulfite treatment of BS-seq is extremely detrimental to RNA, thus resulting in unstable detection of m5C in low abundance RNA or highly structured RNA, which directly affects the confidence of results (Schaefer et al., 2009; Amort and Lusser, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting limitations of BS-seq.

claim: Antibody-based m5C detection methods are unable to recognize methylation on mRNAs with low abundance and secondary structure.
source: These methods are unable to recognize methylation on mRNAs with low abundance and secondary structure.
evidence: This describes limitations of antibody-based methods based on their technical characteristics.

claim: Antibody-based m5C detection methods are highly dependent on antibody specificity, which usually leads to unspecific binding of RNA and a low amount of m5C-modified regions.
source: Moreover, these methods are highly dependent on antibody specificity, which usually leads to unspecific binding of RNA and a low amount of m5C-modified regions.
evidence: This describes known limitations of antibody-based approaches.

claim: TAWO-seq is capable of m5C analysis but highly depends on the oxidation efficiency of perovskite, which usually causes false positives and unstable conversion.
source: Moreover, TAWO-seq, originally developed for the identification of hm5C, is also capable of m5C analysis, but it highly depends on the oxidation efficiency of perovskite, which usually causes false positives and unstable conversion (Yuan et al., 2019; Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TAWO-seq.

claim: Nanopore-seq can directly map m5C by tracking the characteristic changes of bases but faces challenges of a high error rate.
source: Furthermore, the emerging third-generation sequencing, such as Nanopore-seq, can directly map m5C by tracking the characteristic changes of bases, but it still faces challenges of a high error rate (Harel et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Nanopore sequencing.

claim: ALYREF is the initially recognized nuclear m5C reader that binds directly to m5C sites in mRNA.
source: The RNA-binding protein ALYREF is the initially recognized nuclear m5C reader that binds directly to m5C sites in mRNA and plays key roles in promoting mRNA nuclear export or tumor progression (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: ALYREF plays key roles in promoting mRNA nuclear export or tumor progression.
source: The RNA-binding protein ALYREF is the initially recognized nuclear m5C reader that binds directly to m5C sites in mRNA and plays key roles in promoting mRNA nuclear export or tumor progression (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: YBX1 can recognize m5C-modified mRNA through its cold-shock domain.
source: Another well-known m5C reader, YBX1, can also recognize m5C-modified mRNA through its cold-shock domain and participates in a variety of RNA-dependent events such as mRNA packaging, mRNA stabilization, and translational regulation (Yang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2019 and Chen et al., 2019a.

claim: YBX1 participates in mRNA packaging, mRNA stabilization, and translational regulation.
source: Another well-known m5C reader, YBX1, can also recognize m5C-modified mRNA through its cold-shock domain and participates in a variety of RNA-dependent events such as mRNA packaging, mRNA stabilization, and translational regulation (Yang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2019 and Chen et al., 2019a.

claim: ALYREF and YBX1 had a more prominent binding ability to m5C-modified oligonucleotides compared to unmodified oligonucleotides.
source: RNA affinity chromatography and mass spectrometry analyses using biotin-labeled oligonucleotides with or without m5C were performed in previous reports, which indicated that ALYREF and YBX1 had a more prominent binding ability to m5C-modified oligonucleotides (Yang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: YBX1 can preferentially recognize mRNAs with m5C modifications via key amino acids W65-N70 (WFNVRN).
source: YBX1 can preferentially recognize mRNAs with m5C modifications via key amino acids W65-N70 (WFNVRN) (Chen et al., 2019a), while K171 is essential for the specific binding of ALYREF to m5C sites (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019a.

claim: K171 is essential for the specific binding of ALYREF to m5C sites.
source: YBX1 can preferentially recognize mRNAs with m5C modifications via key amino acids W65-N70 (WFNVRN) (Chen et al., 2019a), while K171 is essential for the specific binding of ALYREF to m5C sites (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations in key amino acids responsible for recognizing m5C binding in ALYREF and YBX1 lead to a significant reduction in their binding levels to m5C-containing oligonucleotides.
source: Previous studies have shown that mutations in key amino acids responsible for recognizing m5C binding in ALYREF and YBX1 lead to a significant reduction in their binding levels to m5C-containing oligonucleotides (Yang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: APOBEC1 can specifically catalyze the deamination of cytosine in single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) or DNA (ssDNA) to uracil.
source: APOBEC1, an evolutionarily conserved family member of APOBEC proteins, can specifically catalyze the deamination of cytosine in single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) or DNA (ssDNA) to uracil (Rosenberg et al., 2011; Qian et al., 1998; Siriwardena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on APOBEC1.

claim: TadA8e induces conversion of adenine to inosine (eventually read as guanine by transcriptases) in ssRNA or ssDNA.
source: TadA8e is an adenine deaminase optimized through reengineering of TadA and it induces conversion of adenine to inosine (eventually read as guanine by transcriptases) in ssRNA or ssDNA (Richter et al., 2020; Gaudelli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TadA8e.

claim: APOBEC1 and TadA8e have been employed for the development of precise and efficient base editors such as CBE and ABE8e.
source: APOBEC1 and TadA8e, with their prominent deamination efficiency, have been employed for the development of precise and efficient base editors such as CBE and ABE8e, which find widespread application in studies related to genome editing (Siriwardena et al., 2016; Richter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on base editors.

claim: DRAM-ABE and DRAM-CBE were properly expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: The results showed that DRAM-ABE and DRAM-CBE were properly expressed in HEK293T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Approximately 60% of cells were GFP-positive after DRAM transfection.
source: In addition, flow cytometry that displayed ∼60% of cells were GFP-positive (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The m5C fraction of RPSA is 75.5%.
source: The deep sequencing results showed that the m5C fraction of RPSA and SZRD1 was 75.5% and 27.25%, respectively (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BS-seq PCR deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The m5C fraction of SZRD1 is 27.25%.
source: The deep sequencing results showed that the m5C fraction of RPSA and SZRD1 was 75.5% and 27.25%, respectively (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BS-seq PCR deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DRAM-ABE induced an A-to-G editing rate of 14.7% near the m5C site in RPSA mRNA.
source: Notably, adenine close to the m5C site in RPSA mRNA was mutated into guanine, resulting in an A-to-G editing rate of 14.7% by DRAM-ABE, whereas this was rarely observed with TadA-8e or DRAMmut-ABE (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DRAM-CBE induced 13.6% C-to-U editing in the vicinity of the m5C site in AP5Z1 mRNA.
source: DRAM-CBE induced C-to-U editing in the vicinity of the m5C site in AP5Z1 mRNA, with 13.6% C-to-U editing, while this effect was significantly reduced with APOBEC1 or DRAMmut-CBE (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The DRAM system is more suitable for mRNA m5C detection than for tRNA or rRNA m5C detection.
source: But Sanger sequencing showed that there was no valid A-to-G/C-to-U mutation detected, which is most likely due to the fact that ALYTEF and YBX1 are mainly responsible for the mRNA m5C binding proteins, and thus the DRAM system is more suitable for the mRNA m5C detection (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of mutations detected in tRNA and rRNA samples.

claim: YBX1 and ALYREF preferentially bound RNAs containing m5C modifications.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Yang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019a), those two m5C readers preferentially bound RNAs containing m5C modifications.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA pull-down experiments and supported by citations.

claim: Mutating key amino acids involved in m5C interaction significantly reduced the binding ability of ALYREF and YBX1 to m5C-modified mRNAs.
source: Furthermore, mutating key amino acids involved in their interaction with m5C significantly reduced their binding ability, indicating that ALYREF and YBX1 exhibit specificity for m5C-methylated mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA pull-down experiments shown in the referenced figures.

claim: NSUN2 and NSUN6 were both identified as m5C methyltransferase of mRNA.
source: NSUN2 (Zhang, 2021) and NSUN6 (Liu et al., 2021), two family members of NOL1/NSUN protein, were both identified as m5C methyltransferase of mRNA (Schumann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: m5C methylation of AP5Z1 is catalyzed by NSUN2.
source: It has been previously demonstrated that m5C methylation of AP5Z1 and RPSA is catalyzed by NSUN2 and NSUN6, respectively (Huang et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: m5C methylation of RPSA is catalyzed by NSUN6.
source: It has been previously demonstrated that m5C methylation of AP5Z1 and RPSA is catalyzed by NSUN2 and NSUN6, respectively (Huang et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: C-to-U or A-to-G mutations near m5C sites were significantly reduced in methyltransferase-deficient cells compared with WT cells.
source: In line with this, Sanger sequencing following RT-PCT showed a significant reduction in C-to-U or A-to-G mutations near the m5C sites in methyltransferase-deficient cells compared with WT cells (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: DRAM-seq editing events were enriched in the vicinity of BS-seq m5C sites.
source: Examination of multiple reported high-confidence RNA m5C sites showed that DRAM-seq editing events were also enriched in the vicinity of the BS-seq sites (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IGV browser traces comparing DRAM-seq and BS-seq data.

claim: Knockout cells exhibited overall rare DRAM-seq editing events close to m5C sites in mRNAs.
source: Moreover, the knockout cells exhibited overall rare DRAM-seq editing events close to m5C sites in other mRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IGV browser traces shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Three biological replicates from each experimental group revealed a strong reproducibility of A-to-G/C-to-U mutations in HEK293T cells expressing DRAM-ABE and DRAM-CBE.
source: A comparison of three biological replicates from each experimental group revealed a strong reproducibility of A-to-G/C-to-U mutations in HEK293T cells expressing DRAM-ABE and DRAM-CBE (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: DRAM-edited mRNAs revealed a high degree of overlap across the three biological replicates.
source: Moreover, the DRAM-edited mRNAs revealed a high degree of overlap across the three biological replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: 55.32% of ALYREF-regulated mRNAs can be detected by the DRAM system.
source: And a recent study by Wang et al. showed that ALYREF deletion affects the expression of 94 mRNAs (Wang et al., 2023), and only 55.32% of these ALYREF-regulated mRNAs can be detected by the DRAM system (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with data from Wang et al., 2023.

claim: DRAM-seq editing events in cells expressing DRAM-ABE and DRAM-CBE were primarily located in the CDS and 3'UTR.
source: Our analysis revealed that DRAM-seq editing events in cells expressing DRAM-ABE and DRAM-CBE were primarily located in the CDS and 3'UTR, indicating a nonrandom distribution of m5C (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by distribution analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: DRAM-seq editing sites showed significant enrichment in the CDS.
source: Moreover, plotting the distribution of DRAM-seq editing sites in mRNA segments (5'UTR, CDS, and 3'UTR) highlighted a significant enrichment in the CDS (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by density map analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The likelihood of editing was notably higher in closer proximity to the m5C sites.
source: Comparative analysis of the DRAM-seq editing sites with the previously published BS-seq m5C sites indicated that the likelihood of editing was notably higher in closer proximity to the m5C sites (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by frequency plot analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The editing window of DRAM exhibited enrichment approximately 20 bp before and after the m5C site.
source: Furthermore, the editing window of DRAM exhibited enrichment approximately 20 bp before and after the m5C site (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by frequency plot analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: AC motifs were the most significantly enriched in DRAM-CBE.
source: Investigation into the sequences surrounding the editing window revealed that AC motifs were the most significantly enriched in DRAM-CBE, whereas (U/C) A motifs were most notably enriched in DRAM-ABE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by motif analysis of DRAM-seq data.

claim: (U/C) A motifs were most notably enriched in DRAM-ABE.
source: Investigation into the sequences surrounding the editing window revealed that AC motifs were the most significantly enriched in DRAM-CBE, whereas (U/C) A motifs were most notably enriched in DRAM-ABE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by motif analysis of DRAM-seq data.

claim: APOBEC1 and TadA-8e samples displayed no significantly enriched motifs, with mutations being more randomly orientated.
source: In contrast, the APOBEC1 and TadA-8e samples displayed no significantly enriched motifs, with mutations being more randomly orientated (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by motif analysis shown in Figures 3J and 3K.

claim: DRAM-seq identified the presence of m5C modifications covering 79.6% of the genes detected by Yang et al., 2017.
source: Our results indicated that DRAM-seq identified the presence of m5C modifications covering 79.6% of the genes detected by Yang et al., 2017, and 91.9% of the genes detected by Huang et al., 2019 (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram comparison shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DRAM-seq identified the presence of m5C modifications covering 91.9% of the genes detected by Huang et al., 2019.
source: Our results indicated that DRAM-seq identified the presence of m5C modifications covering 79.6% of the genes detected by Yang et al., 2017, and 91.9% of the genes detected by Huang et al., 2019 (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram comparison shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ATG16L1 coordinates autophagy pathway.
source: Remarkably, certain pivotal regulators with diverse biological functions, such as ATG16L1 (coordinates autophagy pathway) (Fletcher et al., 2018) and ARHGEF25 (plays an important role in actin cytoskeleton reorganization) (Guo et al., 2003), were identified by Zhang et al. and DRAM-seq, but not by Yang et al. (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fletcher et al., 2018.

claim: ARHGEF25 plays an important role in actin cytoskeleton reorganization.
source: Remarkably, certain pivotal regulators with diverse biological functions, such as ATG16L1 (coordinates autophagy pathway) (Fletcher et al., 2018) and ARHGEF25 (plays an important role in actin cytoskeleton reorganization) (Guo et al., 2003), were identified by Zhang et al. and DRAM-seq, but not by Yang et al. (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2003.

claim: FANCD2 maintains chromosome stability.
source: Conversely, FANCD2 (maintains chromosome stability) (Naim and Rosselli, 2009) and RPL15 (components of the large ribosomal subunit) (Anger et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2020) were discovered by Yang et al. and DRAM-seq, but not by Zhang et al. (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naim and Rosselli, 2009.

claim: RPL15 is a component of the large ribosomal subunit.
source: Conversely, FANCD2 (maintains chromosome stability) (Naim and Rosselli, 2009) and RPL15 (components of the large ribosomal subunit) (Anger et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2020) were discovered by Yang et al. and DRAM-seq, but not by Zhang et al. (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anger et al., 2013 and Liang et al., 2020.

claim: m5C RNA-modified genes are involved in the regulation of diverse key biological processes including cell division, cell cycle, mRNA splicing, protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, nucleocytoplasmic transport, translation, and DNA repair.
source: These results highlighted the involvement of these genes in the regulation of diverse key biological processes, such as cell division, cell cycle, mRNA splicing, protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, nucleocytoplasmic transport, translation, DNA repair, and others (Figure 4F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GO and KEGG analyses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: m5C-RIP-seq requires 100–500 ng of RNA.
source: Several experiments have highlighted the requirement of 100–500 ng of RNA for m5C-RIP-seq, while BS-seq necessitates an even more demanding 750–1000 ng of RNA (Huang et al., 2019; Cui et al., 2017; Gu and Liang, 1933).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BS-seq necessitates 750–1000 ng of RNA.
source: Several experiments have highlighted the requirement of 100–500 ng of RNA for m5C-RIP-seq, while BS-seq necessitates an even more demanding 750–1000 ng of RNA (Huang et al., 2019; Cui et al., 2017; Gu and Liang, 1933).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DRAM successfully generated PCR products of RPSA and AP5Z1 mRNAs from cDNAs corresponding to 250 ng, 50 ng, and 10 ng of total RNA.
source: Remarkably, we successfully generated PCR products of these two mRNAs from cDNAs corresponding to 250 ng, 50 ng, and 10 ng of total RNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental results with diluted RNA samples.

claim: Sanger sequencing demonstrated nearly identical Sanger traces across RNA dilutions of 250 ng, 50 ng, and 10 ng.
source: Quantitative analysis by Sanger sequencing demonstrated nearly identical Sanger traces across these dilutions (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: DRAM expression did not adversely affect cell viability.
source: Importantly, there was no significant difference in the relative proliferative capacity of the cells compared to untransfected cells (NC), indicating that DRAM expression did not adversely affect cell viability (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CCK8 assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The editing efficiency of A-to-G and C-to-U within the m5C region significantly decreased as fusion protein expression diminished.
source: Sanger sequencing revealed that the editing efficiency of A-to-G and C-to-U within the m5C region significantly decreased as fusion protein expression diminished (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gradient transfection experiments shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: The transfection efficiency of the DRAM system is concentration-dependent.
source: These findings suggest that the transfection efficiency of the DRAM system is concentration-dependent and that the ratio of editing efficiency to transfection efficiency may assist in the quantitative analysis of m5C using the DRAM system.
evidence: This is inferred from the gradient transfection experiments.

claim: DRAM-seq covered around 80% of the high-confidence m5C-modified genes detected by BS-seq.
source: Notably, DRAM-seq covered around 80% of the high-confidence m5C-modified genes detected by BS-seq and identified more potential m5C sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with BS-seq datasets.

claim: DRAM-seq identified more potential m5C sites than BS-seq.
source: Notably, DRAM-seq covered around 80% of the high-confidence m5C-modified genes detected by BS-seq and identified more potential m5C sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with BS-seq datasets.

claim: DRAM avoids bisulfite treatment, preventing RNA damage and ensuring a more comprehensive representation of RNA samples.
source: This can be attributed to the avoidance of bisulfite treatment by DRAM-seq, preventing RNA damage and ensuring a more comprehensive representation of RNA samples.
evidence: This is inferred from the technical characteristics of DRAM compared to BS-seq.

claim: DRAM requires as low as 10 ng of total RNA for m5C detection.
source: Our analysis demonstrates that DRAM requires as low as 10 ng of total RNA for m5C detection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental results with low-input RNA samples.

claim: The measuring resolution of DRAM is around 40 nt.
source: However, our present study proved that the measuring resolution of DRAM is around 40 nt, which facilitates higher precision than that of m5C-RIP-seq (~100 nt).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of DRAM-seq editing windows.

claim: m5C-RIP-seq has a measuring resolution of approximately 100 nt.
source: However, our present study proved that the measuring resolution of DRAM is around 40 nt, which facilitates higher precision than that of m5C-RIP-seq (~100 nt).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to DRAM's resolution.

claim: DRAM system depends on the specific recognition of m5C modifications on ssRNA by the reader protein.
source: In addition, the DRAM system depends on the specific recognition of m5C modifications on ssRNA by the reader protein, theoretically avoiding the false-positive effects of 5-hydroxymethylation modifications in other assays, such as BS-seq (Huang et al., 2019; Trixl et al., 2019; Schaefer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of DRAM and comparison with BS-seq.

claim: m5C sites are predominantly distributed in the coding sequences (CDS) and notably enriched near the initiation codon.
source: Previous studies have indicated that m5C sites are predominantly distributed in the coding sequences (CDS) and notably enriched near the initiation codon (Yang et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2017; Edelheit et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2020; Squires et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: There is no uniform intrinsic signature motif sequence that can characterize all m5C sites.
source: Previous studies have indicated that there is no uniform intrinsic signature motif sequence that can characterize all m5C sites (Yang et al., 2017; Edelheit et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
